summary: Steel tower on Sooes Peak, dated 1957 (built, or moved from Neah Lookout); down by 1973, footings and ruins remain on Makah land; visit needs permission.

facts.design: Steel tower with cabin; sources give 90 ft (register, Firelookout) or 80 ft (Neah record, Willhite)
facts.status_note: Tower down by 1973; tower footings and ruins reported on the summit
facts.agency: Washington Division of Forestry/DNR (register and Firelookout)

access.note: Access is on Makah tribal land; Willhite says do not visit without permission and the Makah Recreation Pass does not cover the forest roads

events.note: Register gives 1957 as the build year of a 90-foot steel tower and cabin; Willhite and the Neah record instead say the steel tower was moved there that year
Steel tower moved from Neah Lookout (lower elevation) to the Sooes summit
Newspaper item said seven lookouts would be manned in June 1964, Sooes among them; a planned season, not confirmed as staffed
Sources differ: gone by 1973 (register), destroyed (Firelookout), dropped or fell (Willhite), taken down (Neah record)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Register and Firelookout say 90 feet; Neah record and Willhite say 80 feet. The story reports both and picks neither; height_m is left out.
Register says the tower was built at the site in 1957; Willhite and the Neah record say it was moved there from Neah Lookout, a tower Willhite dates to 1942. The story gives both accounts.
Gone by 1973 (register), destroyed (Firelookout), dropped or fell (Willhite), taken down and left lying (Neah record). The story reports each account without choosing one.
Register and Firelookout list the Washington Division of Forestry/DNR; Willhite places the access on Makah tribal land. The sources do not reconcile the two, and the story says so.

sources.title: Sooes Mountain
sources.publisher: Washington Lookouts (forest lookout index, quoting Port Angeles Evening News, April 7, 1964)

notes_for_editor: Sources conflict on height (80 vs 90 ft), origin (built in place vs moved from Neah Lookout) and fate wording; the story reports each. The 1964 item is a planned June season, not proof of who staffed it. No fire history found in these sources. Willhite's 2017 photo captions are the only description of what remains; no recent visit report found. Access is taken from Willhite's note that the land is Makah tribal land.
